title: Fabricated scientists and studies. Court imposes Estonia's first AI fine for AI hallucinations

reading.body:
This is a hallucination failure in a document drafted for a legal proceeding. The model produced citations to academic studies and named researchers that did not exist, and those citations were carried into a filing submitted to a court. The failure surfaced at the point of use, when the court could not locate the studies or the researchers, not at the point of generation.

The case shows a system used without a verification step. Nothing in the reporting indicates the plaintiffs checked the cited research before filing, and the court's position is that responsibility for accuracy rests with the person who signs the document. Catching this would have required searching for the named researchers and the cited studies, a check that does not depend on access to the model or its internals.

The court treated the submission as a matter of party responsibility rather than tool failure, and it noted that AI use in filings is increasing while every submission still requires full review. What is not established is intent: the plaintiffs said they did not mean to mislead, and the court's fines rest on a statutory standard of knowledge or gross negligence, which is a finding the reports attribute to the court rather than an admission by the plaintiffs.

summary:
A Tallinn court fined ten plaintiffs after they submitted a legal filing citing academic studies that did not exist, which were generated by artificial intelligence. The plaintiffs were challenging a logging permit and cited research on clearcutting. The court found the Estonian researchers named in the filing were not real and the studies could not be located. One plaintiff was fined 150 euros and the other nine 50 euros each. The plaintiffs said AI use is not banned and that they did not mean to mislead the court.

The court said AI use is allowed but users are responsible for the accuracy of their claims, since AI tools can produce false information. Court chair Kaupo Kruusvee said AI use in filings is growing and can slow proceedings because every submission still needs full review. He said courts do not use AI to draft decisions. Under Estonian law, courts may fine parties who knowingly or through gross negligence submit false claims. This was Estonia's first known case of fines over AI-generated content in a filing.
